newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: FOCUS-Kazakhs to raise $200-250 mln on international market.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kazakhs to raise $200-250 mln on international market.

text.p: Kazakhstan plans to raise $200-250 million on international markets this autumn, vowing to accept some future hardship to resolve current acute social problems, Prime Minister Akezhan Kazhegeldin said on Wednesday.

"The government is planning this loan, amd therefore we are watching the rates of the yen, mark and the dollar on foreign markets. The borrowing will be no less than $200-250 million, and this will probably happen in autumn," Kazhegeldin said.

Kazhegeldin said the loan would help pay off by January 1 huge debts to Kazakh pensioners which total around $500 million. "We propose to make payments to today's pensioners at the expense of future generations and the future economy," he said.

But the premier said the borrowing would not be burdensome for Kazakhstan's current economy. "Realistically, Kazakhstan can borrow today even $1 billion -- such are the offers from finance companies," he said.
But he added the oil-rich former Soviet republic would only cautiously build up its debt.

Last December the Central Asian state tapped international markets with its debut $200-million Eurobond, which was snapped up by investors. The three-year bond, organised by Dutch bank ABN AMRO Hoare Govett, was priced to yield 9.3 percent or 350 basis points above comparable U.S. treasury notes.
But Kazhegeldin said the government expected to receive a new higher sovereign debt rating from international agencies which would make the loan cheaper.
"I think, the new rating could be assigned in August or September," Kazhegeldin said.
Last year Moody's assigned Kazakhstan a Ba3 sovereign rating for long-term foreign-currency bonds. Agencies IBCA and Standard and Poor's both gave BB-.
"Kazakhstan's current rating was underestimated due to delays with the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC)...But we hope the (CPC) documents will be signed on May 16," the premier said.
The CPC will build a 1,580 km (1,000 mile) pipeline to Russia's Black Sea oil export outlet Novorossiisk from the giant Tengiz oil field in the north-west of land-locked Kazakhstan.
"The infrastructure issue has been a very serious constraint on Western oil industry investment in Kazakhstan," concurred Stephen O'Sullivan, oil and gas analyst at MC Securities LTD in London.
The signing which will take place in Moscow is expected to push the $2 billion project to the development stage.
Russia owns 24 percent of CPC, Kazakhstan 19 percent and Oman seven percent.

The remaining 50 percent is divided among Chevron Corp with 15 percent, Russia's LUKoil LKOH.RTS, Mobil Corp and Russia's Rosneft with 7.5 percent each, British Gas Plc and Italy's Agip SpA with two percent each, and Oryx Energy Company and the state company Kazakh Oil with 1.75 percent each.
CPC, set up in 1992, plans a pipeline with an initial capacity of 28 million tonnes a year (560,000 barrels per day) and a peak of 67 million tonnes a year (1.34 million bpd).
"The issue of further investment in the oil and gas sectors is now the issue of the pipeline," Kazhegeldin said.
